power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.5255", "p = 0.1384 ", "p = 0.1739" ), Sentence = c("Compared to mock-treated embryos (n = 47), infected blastocysts (n = 48) showed a significantly reduced surface area (p = 0.0003), reduced total cell number (p = 0.0139), and reduced NANOG + epiblast cell numbers (p = 0.0054) 24 hours post-exposure, while the number of GATA4 + primitive endoderm cells remained unaffected (p = 0.5255).", "The antiviral genes IFIH1 and IRF7 showed a trend toward increased expression that did not reach significance in this paired comparison (p = 0.1384 and p = 0.1739, respectively).", "The antiviral genes IFIH1 and IRF7 showed a trend toward increased expression that did not reach significance in this paired comparison (p = 0.1384 and p = 0.1739, respectively)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Human preimplantation embryos express the SARS-CoV-2 entry factors ACE2, TMPRSS2 and BSG (CD147) on trophectoderm (TE) cells, suggesting susceptibility to infection.
Likewise, SARS-CoV-2-pseudotyped reporter viruses induced cytopathic effects in blastocysts, while the zona pellucida (ZP) appeared to confer partial protection.
The impact of authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection on embryonic lineage specification and developmental competence has not been established.
Here, we exposed cryopreserved human embryos, donated under ethics approval and informed consent, to authentic SARS-CoV-2 (B.1.617.2, Delta variant).
While embryos with an intact ZP remained uninfected, laser-assisted hatching rendered 19/21 (90.5%) of embryos susceptible to infection, as confirmed by detection of viral dsRNA.
Moreover, SARS-CoV-2 infection had a pronounced effect on blastocyst development with a possibly fatal outcome.

Compared to mock-treated embryos (n = 47), infected blastocysts (n = 48) showed a significantly reduced surface area (p = 0.0003), reduced total cell number (p = 0.0139), and reduced NANOG + epiblast cell numbers (p = 0.0054) 24 hours post-exposure, while the number of GATA4 + primitive endoderm cells remained unaffected (p = 0.5255).

Intriguingly, despite viral replication being largely confined to the trophectoderm (TE), this selective epiblast reduction suggests a disruption of TE-derived paracrine signaling required for epiblast specification.
Finally, prolonged viral replication resulted in embryonic lysis and death.

Digital transcriptomic profiling (mock, n = 29 embryos; SARS-CoV-2, n = 28 embryos; each in n = 5 minipools) revealed upregulation of innate antiviral and inflammatory genes, including IFIH1, IRF7, NOD2, and TNFRSF1A, as well as the recently identified SARS-CoV-2 entry factor TMEM106B, alongside altered developmental signatures concerning genome activation, pluripotency, and lineage-specific programs.

These findings show that ZP disruption makes human blastocysts susceptible to productive SARS-CoV-2 infection, with adverse consequences for lineage allocation and direct implications for biosafety and virological counselling in medically assisted reproduction practice.

When SARS-CoV-2 appeared as a global health emergency in early 2020, its rapid spread posed an unprecedented challenge to healthcare systems worldwide, causing excess morbidity and mortality and disrupting medical care across virtually all specialties.

Among the populations of particular concern were pregnant women and those undergoing medically assisted reproduction (MAR): clinicians and patients facing infertility treatment confronted an immediate and unanswered question: was it safe to continue 1 ?

As clinical experience accumulated, evidence suggested that MAR technologies could generally be performed safely following recovery from SARS-CoV-2 infection, with clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, and live birth rates largely comparable to those of uninfected patients 2.

text.text: However, several studies reported reductions in embryo quality with molecular profiles of developmental delay, and an increase in miscarriage rate following recent infection, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood [2] [3] [4] .

text.text: Moreover, clinical outcome studies cannot determine whether these observations result from direct viral effects on the embryo or indirect maternal and endometrial factors, underscoring the need for experimental models that specifically address embryonic susceptibility to infection.

Beyond the preimplantation period, SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, including preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, placental pathology, and stillbirth 5 .

text.text: The severity of these complications differed between SARS-CoV-2 variants.

Epidemiological studies consistently identified the Delta (B.1.617.2) variant of concern as being associated with the highest risk of severe maternal disease and adverse perinatal outcomes compared with earlier and subsequent variants 6, 7 .

text.text: Consequently, the Delta variant represents a clinically relevant model for investigating the effects of SARS-CoV-2 on early human development.

While these complications have been extensively investigated during established pregnancy, little is known about the effects of viral exposure before implantation, a question particularly relevant to MAR, where human gametes and embryos are manipulated outside the maternal environment and may be exposed to infectious agents during laboratory procedures.

Although embryos are cultured under highly controlled conditions 8 , procedures such as oocyte retrieval, oocyte denudation (enzymatic softening and mechanical stripping of the cumulus and corona cells from an egg), embryo culture, assisted hatching, trophectoderm (TE) biopsy, and cryopreservation can transiently compromise their natural barriers.

text.text: As the blastocyst expands, mechanical pressure combined with enzymatic degradation by TE-secreted and uterine proteases causes the ZP to thin and rupture, a process termed hatching, typically occurring at 5-6 dpf 18, 19 .

text.text: Hatching precedes implantation.
It enables direct contact between the TE and the endometrial epithelium, thereby facilitating blastocyst apposition, adhesion, and subsequent invasion into the endometrium.

However, hatching also marks the loss of the embryo's protective shell, exposing the conceptus directly to the uterine environment for the first time, a vulnerability that becomes particularly relevant when considering exposure to infectious agents.

A molecular basis for embryo susceptibility was established when the entry receptors angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), Basigin (BSG/CD147), and transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2), the principal host factors mediating SARS-CoV-2 cell entry, were detected on TE cells of human blastocysts, suggesting that preimplantation embryos possess the machinery required for viral infection 20, 21 .

While the above study modeled direct viral exposure in vitro, subsequent studies examined embryos derived from mothers with acute infection and found evidence of impaired . development in more detail.

Surplus cryopreserved embryos were donated to research, after informed written consent and 5 years of cryopreservation, by patients who had completed their fertility treatment at Brussels IVF (UZ Brussel) and no longer needed them.

text.text: Briefly, 3 dpf (8-12 cell stage) embryos and 5 dpf (blastocyst stage) embryos, the latter derived from preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) cycles and therefore already possessing a ZP opened using LAH, were warmed using the Vit Kit-Thaw kit (90137-SO, Irvine Scientific) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

The 3 dpf embryos were cultured in equilibrated 25 μl droplets of blastocyst medium (83060010, ORIGIO Sequential Blast, with phenol red) overlaid with Ovoil (10174, Vitrolife) to prevent evaporation, at 37 °C, 5% O2, and 6% CO2 in a G185 flatbed incubator (K-Systems, CooperSurgical) for 24 h until 4 dpf before transport to the BSL-3 facility at the Rega Institute (KU Leuven).
The 5 dpf embryos were allowed a 2-hour recovery period after warming before further transport.

Only embryos that resumed development after cryopreservation were used in subsequent experiments; embryos showing signs of degeneration (including cytoplasmic vacuolization, cellular fragmentation, or cell lysis) in more than one cell were discarded.
No clinical information on the donors, including maternal conditions or the indication for PGT, was available, and these factors could therefore not be accounted for in the analysis.

Following culture or recovery, embryos were transferred into microvials (5000-1020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing pre-equilibrated blastocyst medium and placed in a G95 Portable Incubator (K-Systems, CooperSurgical) at 37 °C for transport to the BSL-3 facility.
There, embryos were immediately recovered from the microvials into fresh, pre-equilibrated 25 μl droplets under the same culture conditions.

The 4 dpf embryos were cultured for a further 24 h until reaching the 5 dpf blastocyst stage before assignment to experimental groups; the 5 dpf embryos were randomly assigned to experimental groups directly following transport and reequilibration.

Embryos from the same experiment were warmed, cultured, and infected on the same day under identical conditions, so that each infected group had a matched mock group, and were subsequently allocated to downstream analysis by immunofluorescence or nCounter-based transcriptomic profiling; for the latter, embryos were transferred into 20 μl RLT lysis buffer (Qiagen) and snap-frozen.
For the 3 dpf embryo groups, the ZP was opened by either laser-assisted hatching (LAH) or removed by chemical treatment with acid Tyrode's solution (TS, pH 2.5 ± 0.3; T1788, Sigma-Aldrich).
LAH was performed as previously described 27 .

text.text: Briefly, embryos were immobilized with the ZP positioned in the focal plane, and a series of consecutive laser pulses (80% intensity, millisecond-range pulse duration) was applied to a region distant from the blastomeres to create an opening of approximately 20 µm.
Care was taken to avoid direct laser exposure of embryonic cells, after which the embryos were washed and returned to culture.

Chemical ZP removal was performed in 50 μl microdroplets of acid Tyrode's solution or HEPES (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid; H6147, Sigma-Aldrich) medium supplemented with human serum albumin, under an Ivesta 3 Greenough stereomicroscope with integrated camera (Leica).
Embryos were first rinsed in HEPES medium by gentle pipetting, then transferred to an acid droplet, where the outer zona layer was dissolved by gentle pipetting under continuous observation.
Once the outer layer was nearly fully dissolved, pipetting was stopped immediately to avoid damaging the embryo.
Embryos were then washed three times in HEPES medium and transferred to a new culture dish.

text.text: Donated 3 dpf embryos were warmed at IVF Brussel and assigned to one of three groups.
In the LAH group, partial ZP ablation was performed on the day of warming after embryo recovery.

In the TS group, the ZP likewise remained intact at this stage.
All three groups were cultured to 4 dpf and transported to the BSL-3 facility, where TS-designated embryos underwent gentle chemical ZP removal following a 2-hour recovery period.
Culture then continued to 5 dpf, when embryos were randomly assigned to SARS-CoV-2 or mock infection.
Untreated, ZP-intact embryos were challenged with 3x10⁵ TCID50/ml of the SARS-CoV-2 (Delta) variant, whereas LAH-and TS-treated embryos were infected with 3x10⁴ TCID50/ml.
All embryos were fixed 24 hours post-infection (hpi) for immunofluorescence analysis.

The response appeared to be stronger in pools with higher viral transcript abundance than in pools with few viral transcripts, although this was not formally tested.

Across several developmental programs, module scores were consistently higher in infected pools, most clearly in the cohorts with the highest viral transcript abundance.

None of these differences reached statistical significance after correction for multiple testing, and because transcriptomes were measured in pools of embryos from five matched experiments, the results reflect average responses and should be considered exploratory.
Nevertheless, they raise the possibility that SARS-CoV-2 infection is accompanied by shifts in embryonic transcriptional state, and they provide effect-size estimates for designing larger studies.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of individual embryos, together with a panel that covers developmental genes, would show which cells and lineages are affected and whether the response is uniform across embryos, and functional analysis of embryo development after infection would test whether these shifts have consequences.
While LAH consistently resulted in efficient viral infection, TS treatment frequently left residual zona material surrounding the embryo, substantially reducing infection efficiency.

This observation is consistent with the bilayered structure of the human ZP, in which the outer layer is more readily dissolved while the compact inner layer is considerably more resistant to acidic digestion 42, 43 .

text.text: Beyond explaining the lower infection rate observed after Tyrode treatment, this offers a practical methodological consideration for future studies of pathogen interactions with human embryos and for investigating differences in the physiological function of individual ZP layers.
Notably, all but one embryo with an intact ZP remained protected.

The exception showed viral replication despite apparently preserved zona integrity, but had previously undergone ICSI, suggesting that even submicroscopic discontinuities as created by microneedle puncture during microinjection may suffice to permit viral access, raising the possibility that any experimental procedure compromising ZP integrity may influence susceptibility.

Following ZP disruption, SARS-CoV-2 infection impaired blastocyst development, as evidenced by reduced embryo expansion, decreased total cell number, and a selective reduction in NANOG-positive epiblast cells, while GATA4-positive primitive endoderm cell numbers remained unchanged.

The overall reduction in embryo growth is consistent with a generalized developmental impairment, whereas the disproportionate loss of epiblast cells suggests that this lineage may be particularly vulnerable to the downstream consequences of infection.

Because viral replication was predominantly observed within the TE cell lineage, these developmental alterations are unlikely to result solely from direct infection of the embryonic lineages themselves but rather from a broader perturbation of the overall developmental program.
A plausible explanation is that SARS-CoV-2 infection disrupts the paracrine communication between the TE and the ICM.

Beyond its structural role in blastocyst formation, the TE functions as an important signaling niche for the ICM by secreting factors such as IL-6 that support normal blastocyst development and lineage progression 44 .

text.text: In addition, TE-derived cells possess a functional type I interferon system capable of protecting embryonic stem cells through paracrine signaling, whereas embryonic stem cells themselves exhibit limited capacity to produce antiviral interferons 45 .

text.text: Disruption of this supportive relationship by viral infection therefore represents a possible mechanistic link by which TE infection could selectively impair epiblast development without requiring direct viral replication within the epiblast.

For example, infection of pre-and peri-implantation embryos with teratogenic Zika virus was largely restricted to the TE yet was sufficient to impair subsequent embryonic and fetal development 46 , supporting the concept that dysfunction of this extraembryonic lineage can influence embryonic development even in the absence of direct infection of the epiblast.

text.text: This evidence is indirect, as it comes from other models and was not designed to test TE-epiblast signaling, and this mechanism was not tested in the present study; it should therefore be seen as a hypothesis.
Alternative explanations should also be considered.
The epiblast may be intrinsically more sensitive than the primitive endoderm to inflammatory stress induced by viral infection.
Similarly, the observed phenotype may reflect a generalized developmental delay that disproportionately affects the rapidly expanding epiblast population.
The present study cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

Future research combining lineage-specific viral detection with single-cell transcriptomics and TE-ICM co-culture systems will be important to determine whether disrupted paracrine signaling represents a direct mechanistic link between TE infection and impaired epiblast development.
Transcriptomic profiling further revealed that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces an intrinsic antiviral response in pools of preimplantation embryos.

Increased expression of IFIH1, IRF7, USP18, NOD2, and TNF-associated signaling pathways indicates that embryonic cells can detect viral infection and activate innate immune programs before implantation, consistent with previous evidence that human preimplantation embryos express functional pattern-recognition receptors and respond to pathogen-associated stimuli 47 .

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings.
First, our study evaluated a single SARS-CoV-2 variant, Delta (B.1.617.2), and viral entry or replication characteristics may differ between variants.

However, the latter variant may serve as a representative prototype, given that the Delta variant, which became the dominant global strain by mid-to-late 2021 and drove a surge in infections, exhibited a particularly strong impact on reproductive health 6 .

text.text: Moreover, the direct and timed exposure of ZP-disrupted embryos to a defined viral inoculum does not recapitulate the complex conditions of natural conception.
The in vitro system further lacks maternal immune, endocrine, and uterine interactions that shape early pregnancy.
Either contribution will need to be studied in future experiments, for which we herewith provide a base dataset.
In addition, infection was confirmed by dsRNA staining, which indicates viral replication but does not quantify the level of infection per embryo.
Second, digital transcriptomics (nCounter) is a targeted method.

The panel used here focuses on innate immunity and was not designed for early embryonic or pregnancy development, so genes relevant to these processes may have been missed, and novel transcripts or pathways cannot be identified.
Its sensitivity, of digital transcriptomics, though possibly equally, if not more, sensitive than other methodologies such as RNA sequencing 60 is also limited.

text.text: While use of minipools may have helped average experimental errors between biological replicates, a striking inter-cohort variability remains.

Likewise, the limited number of pools available for transcriptomic analysis resulted in reduced statistical power for exploratory pathway and developmental module analyses; therefore, these findings require validation in larger cohorts.

Nevertheless, disruption of certain transcriptional patterns linked to an established pseudotime of early development suggests a risk of loss of lineage commitment and stage-specific vulnerabilities 12 .

text.text: However, pinpointing such specific vulnerabilities should be feasible from transcriptional data sets as presented herein.

Third, the embryos were surplus embryos donated to research, and no clinical background information on the donors, such as maternal conditions or the indication for PGT, was available, and the sex of the embryos was unknown.
These factors could therefore not be taken into account.
Random allocation of embryos to matched mock and infected groups within each experiment was used so that such variability would be distributed across both groups.
Finally, although our data support a model in which TE infection indirectly affects epiblast development, the underlying mechanisms remain to be established.
Targeted disruption of developmental programs, such as by viral infection in the current study, may help elucidate such natural dependencies.
The in vitro system also cannot capture maternal factors or assess longer-term consequences after implantation, which will require further investigation.
In conclusion, our findings identify the human ZP as the principal barrier preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection of preimplantation embryos.
Once this barrier is disrupted, authentic SARS-CoV-2 readily infects blastocysts, impairs embryonic growth, selectively affects epiblast development, and induces a cell-intrinsic antiviral response.

While direct embryonic infection during natural conception is likely uncommon, these findings provide mechanistic insight into early embryonic susceptibility to viral infection and underscore the importance of maintaining appropriate biosafety considerations during MAR procedures.

Only five experiments were analyzed, and embryos had to be pooled because a single embryo does not yield enough RNA for detection, so individual embryos could not be studied; our conclusions are therefore preliminary.

The variability we observed between experiments may partly reflect the natural biological variability of human embryos, which should be kept in mind when interpreting responses to viral infection.While our experimental model demonstrates that human blastocysts can support SARS-CoV-2 infection as soon as the ZP barrier is compromised, the relevance of this scenario to natural conception requires careful consideration.
Additional physiological barriers can be expected to limit infection of the embryo during natural conception.

The intact ZP physically isolates the preimplantation embryo during transit through the reproductive tract, and productive SARS-CoV-2 infection of the female reproductive tract itself appears uncommon.
Indeed, viral mRNA was undetectable in endometrial biopsies from women with active COVID-19 despite ACE2 expression in this tissue50 .
text.formatted: Indeed, viral mRNA was undetectable in endometrial biopsies from women with active COVID-19 despite ACE2 expression in this tissue<ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> .

text.text: Although SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been sporadically detected in semen and reproductive tissues, studies in acute COVID-19 have generally failed to demonstrate consistent seminal shedding51 .

text.text: Detection of viral RNA in semen from some individuals with Long COVID has raised the possibility of persistent reproductive tract reservoirs52 .

text.text: However, whether this represents infectious virus with implications for fertility and transmission remains unresolved.Embryonic infection in vivo would additionally require a tightly synchronized sequence of events, including maternal infection during the narrow preimplantation window and sufficient viral dissemination to the uterine environment before implantation.

Direct embryonic infection during natural conception is therefore likely rare; adverse reproductive outcomes associated with maternal COVID-19 more plausibly arise through indirect mechanisms, including systemic inflammation, cytokine dysregulation, altered endometrial receptivity, or placental dysfunction after implantation[53] [54] [55] .
text.formatted: Direct embryonic infection during natural conception is therefore likely rare; adverse reproductive outcomes associated with maternal COVID-19 more plausibly arise through indirect mechanisms, including systemic inflammation, cytokine dysregulation, altered endometrial receptivity, or placental dysfunction after implantation<ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref> .

text.text: Maternal immune activation may represent an additional mechanism by which infection can influence early development.

Although a controlled inflammatory response is an integral part of implantation and early pregnancy, excessive or dysregulated production of inflammatory mediators can disrupt the cellular and molecular processes required for normal embryonic development56, 57 .
text.formatted: Although a controlled inflammatory response is an integral part of implantation and early pregnancy, excessive or dysregulated production of inflammatory mediators can disrupt the cellular and molecular processes required for normal embryonic development<ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> .

text.text: Thus, even in the absence of direct embryonic infection, maternal infection-associated inflammation may create an adverse developmental environment during critical windows of early pregnancy.The implications may differ in MAR settings, where procedures such as LAH or ICSI intentionally breach the ZP.

Laboratory transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is considered extremely unlikely under modern biosafety protocols58, 59 , but our findings show that embryos become susceptible once this physical barrier is compromised.
text.formatted: Laboratory transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is considered extremely unlikely under modern biosafety protocols<ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> , but our findings show that embryos become susceptible once this physical barrier is compromised.

text.text: The viral inoculum used here was chosen to establish a reliable experimental infection and does not reflect typical clinical exposure levels; the consequences of lower-dose exposure, and whether limited viral replication could influence implantation, lineage specification, or later fetal development, remain open questions.
Importantly, these findings do not suggest that routine IVF procedures pose a substantial risk of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, or viral infections in general.
Nevertheless, they highlight the importance of understanding how specific micromanipulation procedures may alter the physical barriers that normally protect the embryo.
Several experiments could validate our main conclusions.

First, repeating the single-cell RNA sequencing approach used to define the developmental modules 12 on infected and mock embryos would show which cells and lineages respond, and whether the response is uniform across embryos.
Second, following individual embryos, with measurement of their development, lineage composition, and gene expression, would link infection directly to fate, which pooling did not allow.
Third, larger cohorts, other viral variants, and quantitative measurement of infection in each embryo would test whether the response depends on the amount of virus.
